pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Anti-NMDA Receptor Encephalitis secondary to Mature Ovarian Teratoma THE SMOKING GUN: The multi-stage progression in a young female from acute psychosis to pathognomonic orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, and hypoventilation, coupled with a calcified ovarian mass (dermoid cyst/teratoma) on pelvic imaging. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: This severe autoimmune encephalitis is driven by IgG autoantibodies targeted against the GluN1 subunit of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. In young females, the trigger is frequently a mature ovarian teratoma containing nervous tissue. The immune system mounts a response against the foreign neuronal tissue inside the teratoma, producing cross-reactive antibodies that breach the blood-brain barrier. These autoantibodies bind to NMDA receptors in the forebrain and hippocampus, causing cross-linking and internalising of the receptors. The resulting state of NMDA receptor hypofunction disrupts frontostriatal circuits, triggering a predictable sequential progression: initial psychiatric symptoms, extrapyramidal movement disorders, seizures, central hypoventilation, and life-threatening autonomic storms. Definitive treatment requires surgical resection of the ovarian teratoma along with aggressive immunotherapy (IVIG, plasmapheresis, steroids, and rituximab).
